'''''Buddleja davidii''''' (spelling variant ''Buddleia davidii''), also called '''butterfly-bush''',<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web | title=Butterfly-bush ''Buddleja davidii'' Franch. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.xy | access-date=2025-12-09}}</ref> '''orange eye''', or '''summer lilac''', is a [[species]] of flowering plant in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Scrophulariaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to most of China except for the far northeast.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=''Buddleja davidii'' Franch. | website=Plants of the World Online | date=2020-09-11 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:545734-1 | access-date=2025-12-09}}</ref> It is widely used as an [[ornamental plant]], and many named [[cultivar]]s are in cultivation. The genus was named ''Buddleja'' after the English botanist, Reverend [[Adam Buddle]]. The [[species name]], ''davidii'', is after the French missionary and explorer in China, Father [[Armand David]], who was the first European to report the shrub.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Buddleja davidii - Plant Finder|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=271488&isprofile=1&basic=buddleja%20davidii|access-date=2021-02-18|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> It was found near [[Yichang]] by Dr [[Augustine Henry]] about 1887 and sent to St Petersburg. Another botanist-missionary in China, [[Jean-André Soulié]], sent seed to the French nursery [[Vilmorin]], and ''B. davidii'' entered commerce in the 1890s.<ref>Alice M. Coats, ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'' (1964) 1992, ''s.v.'' "Buddleia"</ref>

''B. davidii'' was accorded the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]] [[Award of Merit]] (AM) in 1898, and the [[Award of Garden Merit]] (AGM) in 1941.<ref name=Hillier>Hillier & Sons. (1990). ''Hillier's Manual of Trees & Shrubs, 5th ed.''. p. 47. David & Charles, Newton Abbot. {{ISBN|0-7153-67447}}</ref>

==Description==
''Buddleja davidii'' is a vigorous shrub with an arching habit, growing to {{convert|5|m|0|abbr=on}} in height. The pale grey-brown bark becomes flaky to deeply fissured with age. The branches are quadrangular in section, the younger shoots and leaves covered in a dense [[indumentum]]. The opposite [[leaf shape|lanceolate]] leaves are {{convert|7|-|20|cm|in|0|abbr=in}} long and {{convert|2|-|7|cm|in|0|abbr=in}} broad, grey-green to dark green above, greyish-white tomentose beneath when young and becoming grey-green with age. The flowers are honey-scented, lilac to purple or occasionally white, produced in terminal [[panicle]]s, usually under {{convert|20|cm|in|0|abbr=in}} long but can be {{convert|30|cm|in|0|abbr=in}} or more long.<ref name="RHSD">{{cite book | last1=Huxley | first1=Anthony | title=Royal Horticultural Society Dictionary of Gardening | publisher=Macmillan Stockton press | publication-place=London New York | date=1992 | isbn=1-56159-001-0 |volume=1 | page=411 }}</ref><ref name=Stuart,1>Stuart, D. (2006). ''Buddlejas''. pp 30–34. RHS Plant Collector Series, Timber Press, Oregon. {{ISBN|978-0-88192-688-0}}</ref> The flowers are [[Plant sexuality|perfect]] (having both male and female parts), hence are [[hermaphrodite]] rather than [[monoecious]] (separate male and female flowers on the same plant) as is often incorrectly stated. [[Ploidy]] 2''n'' = 76 (tetraploid).<ref name=Chen>{{cite journal | last1 = Chen | first1 = G | last2 = Sun | first2 = W-B | last3 = Sun | first3 = H | year = 2007 | title = Ploidy variation in Buddleja L. (Buddlejaceae) in the Sino - Himalayan region and its biogeographical implications | journal = Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society | volume = 154 | issue = 3| pages = 305–312 | doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2007.00650.x| doi-access = free }}</ref> The seeds are very small, and wind-dispersed.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/>

==Cultivation==
''Buddleja davidii'' cultivars are widely cultivated worldwide as ornamental shrubs and for the value of their flowers as a [[nectar]] source for many species of [[butterfly]]. However, the plant does not provide food for butterfly larvae, and buddlejas might out-compete the host plants that caterpillars require.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Zerbe |first1=Leah |title=Why You Should Never Plant a Butterfly Bush Again |url=https://www.goodhousekeeping.com/home/gardening/a20706544/never-plant-butterfly-bush/ |website=Good Housekeeping |publisher=Hearst Media |access-date=2019-10-23 |date=2018-06-18}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Gupta |first1=Tanya |title=Buddleia: The plant that dominates Britain's railways |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-28196221 |website=BBC News |publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=2019-10-23 |date=2014-07-15}}</ref>

The species and its cultivars are not able to survive the harsh winters of northern or [[montane ecosystems|montane climates]], being killed by temperatures below about {{convert|-15|to|-20|C|F}}.{{cn|date=December 2025}}

Younger wood is more [[floriferous]], so even if frosts do not kill the previous year's growth, the shrub can be hard-pruned in spring once frosts have finished, to encourage new growth. The removal of spent flower panicles may be undertaken to reduce the nuisance of self-seeding and encourage further flower production; this extends the flowering season which is otherwise limited to about six weeks, although the flowers of the second and third flushes are invariably smaller.

[[Hardiness zone|Hardiness]]: [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] zones 5–9.<ref name=Stuart,2>Stuart, D. D. (2006). ''Buddlejas''. pp. 119–120. RHS Plant Guide. Timber Press, Oregon. {{ISBN|978-0-88192-688-0}}</ref>

There are approximately 180 ''Buddleja davidii'' [[cultivars]], as well as numerous hybrids, including with ''[[Buddleja globosa]]'' and ''[[Buddleja fallowiana]]'' grown in gardens. Some cultivars are of a dwarf habit, growing to no more than {{convert|1.5|m|ft|0|abbr=in}}. 

A plant-evaluation manager at the [[Chicago Botanic Garden]] in [[Glencoe, Illinois]] (USDA Hardiness zone 5b) rated nearly 50 ''Buddlejia'' varieties and cultivars during a six-year trial period, with a summary in 2015 of the characteristics of each and the study's findings.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Hawke|first=Richard|date=August 2015|url=https://www.chicagobotanic.org/sites/default/files/pdf/plantinfo/buddleja2015.pdf|title=Beyond the basic Butterfly Bush: Plant Trial Results|pages=31–36|magazine=[[Fine Gardening]]|location=[[Newtown, Connecticut]]|publisher=[[Taunton Press]]|access-date=13 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160421032553/http://www.chicagobotanic.org/sites/default/files/pdf/plantinfo/buddleja2015.pdf|archive-date=21 April 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> University studies have suggested that nectaring butterflies have greater preferences for some ''Buddleja'' cultivars than for others, with [[Buddleja Lo & Behold 'Blue Chip'|Lo & Behold 'Blue Chip']] and 'Pink Delight' heading a list of eleven.<ref name="Rutgers">{{cite web|url=https://www.cpe.rutgers.edu/hgs/docs/2018/Workshop-33-Buddleia.pdf|title=Buddleia|location=[[New Brunswick, New Jersey]]|publisher=[[New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station]]: [[Rutgers University|Rutgers]] Office of Continuing Education|access-date=15 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210815200140/https://www.cpe.rutgers.edu/hgs/docs/2018/Workshop-33-Buddleia.pdf|archive-date=15 August 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Other notable cultivars and hybrids include [[Buddleja × weyeriana|'Golden Glow']] and [[Buddleja 'Silver Frost'|'Silver Frost']].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Moore |first=Raymond J. |date=June 1960 |title=Cyto-Taxonomic Notes on Buddleia |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/j.1537-2197.1960.tb10621.x |journal=[[American Journal of Botany]] |volume=47 |issue=6 |pages=511–517 |doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1960.tb10621.x|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Buddleja 'Silver Frost' - Trees and Shrubs Online |url=https://treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/buddleja/buddleja-silver-frost/ |access-date=2021-12-04 |website=treesandshrubsonline.org}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
[[File:Buddleja davidii next to rails at train station Düsseldorf-Zoo.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.0|''Buddleja davidii'' self-sown along a rail line at [[Düsseldorf]], Germany (2016)]]
''Buddleja davidii'' has been designated as an [[invasive species]] or a "[[noxious weed]]" in a number of countries in [[temperate region]]s, including the United Kingdom, the Republic of Ireland and New Zealand.<ref>Multiple sources:
* {{cite web|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/10314|title=Buddleja davidii (butterfly bush)|work=Invasive Species Compendium|year=2021|location=[[Wallingford, Oxfordshire|Wallingford]], [[Oxfordshire]], England|publisher=[[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International]]|access-date=13 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210813174445/https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/10314|archive-date=13 August 2021|url-status=live}}{{cite journal|last1=Dhuill|first1=E.N.|last2=Smyth|first2=N.|year=2021|title=Invasive non-native and alien garden escape plant species on the southern cliffs of Howth, Co. Dublin (H21)|journal=Irish Naturalists| volume=37|issue=2|pages=102–108}}
* {{cite journal|last1=Tallent-Halsell|first1=Nita G.|last2=Watt|first2=Michael S.|date=September 2009|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/226823556|title=The Invasive Buddleja davidii (Butterfly Bush)|jstor=40389400|journal=Botanical Review|doi=10.1007/s12229-009-9033-0|volume=75|issue=3|pages=292–325|s2cid=46039523|location=New York|publisher=[[Springer Publishing|Springer]]|bibcode=2009BotRv..75..292T |access-date=13 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210813225911/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/226823556_The_Invasive_Buddleja_davidii_Butterfly_Bush|archive-date=13 August 2021|url-status=live|via=[[ResearchGate]]}}</ref> It is [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in Australia<ref name="APNI">{{cite web |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/116843 |title=''Buddleja davidii'' |website=[[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI) |publisher=Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, [[Australian Government]] |access-date=3 April 2023}}</ref> and in many cities of central and southern Europe, where it can spread on open land, railway lines, urban areas and in gardens. 

''B. davidii'' was first documented as an invasive species in 1922, in the United Kingdom at [[Harlech]] in North Wales.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> It is now often seen there along railway lines and on the sites of derelict factories and other walls and buildings.<ref>{{cite news|first=Tanya|last=Gupta|date=15 July 2014|title=Buddleia: The plant that dominates Britain's railways|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-28196221|access-date=5 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200408194951/https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-28196221|archive-date=8 April 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> The plant frequently grew on urban bomb sites during the aftermath of [[World War II]], earning it the nickname of "the bomb site plant".<ref>{{cite news|first=Jonathan|last=Moynihan|url=https://patch.com/maryland/edgewater/flower-of-the-week-butterfly-bush-buddleia-davidii|title=Flower of the Week: Butterfly Bush|work=[[Patch (website)|Patch]]|location=[[Edgewater, Maryland|Edgewater]]-[[Davidsonville, Maryland|Davisonville]], [[Maryland]]|access-date=7 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210807152007/https://patch.com/maryland/edgewater/flower-of-the-week-butterfly-bush-buddleia-davidii|archive-date=7 August 2021|url-status=dead|quote=These popular garden flowers can even survive in post-war circumstances, earning the name, "the bomb site plant".}}</ref>

''B. davidii'' is widely marketed throughout the United States, where it has reportedly become invasive in some, but not all, areas within which it has been planted.<ref name=USDA>{{cite web|first=Ann|last=Young-Mathews|year=2011|url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/factsheet/pdf/fs_buda2.pdf|title=Plant fact sheet for orange eye butterflybush (Buddleja davidii)|location=[[Corvallis, Oregon]]|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]]: Corvallis Plant Materials Center|access-date=4 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210804004132/https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/factsheet/pdf/fs_buda2.pdf|archive-date=4 August 2021|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=Hurwitz>{{cite journal|editor-first=Jane|editor-last= Hurwitz|url=https://www.naba.org/pubs/bg172/bg172_Butterflybush_Issue.pdf|title=The Great Butterfly Bush Debate|journal=Butterfly Gardener|volume=7|issue=2|date=Summer 2012|publisher=[[North American Butterfly Association]]|access-date=4 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210722151713/https://www.naba.org/pubs/bg172/bg172_Butterflybush_Issue.pdf|archive-date=22 July 2021|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>Multiple sources:

Peter Podaras developed the "Flutterby" ''Buddleja'' series during the 2000s while at [[New York State College of Agriculture and Life Sciences at Cornell University#History|Cornell University's Department of Horticulture]] in [[Ithaca, New York]] and patented them in 2011. Podaras selected each of the cultivars for their sterility or low fertility. Although innovative when introduced, several members of the series are no longer commercially available and are rare in cultivation.<ref>{{cite web|first=Andrew|last=Large|year=2021|url=https://www.treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/buddleja/buddleja-flutterby-series/|title=Buddleja FLUTTERBY™ Series|work=Trees and Shrubs Online|publisher=International Dendrology Society|access-date=14 February 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002020955/https://www.treesandshrhubsonline.org/articles/buddleja/buddleja-flutterby-series/|archive-date=2 October 2023|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Monarch Watch]]'' recommends planting only male-sterile "Flutterby" cultivars.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.monarchwatch.org/garden/plant-list-monarchwatch.pdf|title=Plants For Butterfly And Pollinator Gardens: Native and Non-native Plants Suitable for Gardens in the Northeastern United States|publisher=[[Monarch Watch]]|access-date=4 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028234109/https://www.monarchwatch.org/garden/plant-list-monarchwatch.pdf|archive-date=28 October 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>
